egress.terms: The basic static residential IPv4 plan now lists 'Shared by up to 3 users', '1 GB bandwidth', 'No speed upgrades', 'No concurrency upgrades' and 'HTTP/SOCKS5'; the 1-month price is $2.71 and the 12-month price is $2.17/month. The old unlimited-bandwidth, 100+ threads and 100+ Mbps bullets are no longer on the page.

interface_detail: HTTP(S) proxy endpoint on a fixed address, ordered per IP from the app.proxy-cheap.com checkout.
tooling: any HTTP proxy client; nothing debrid-specific is needed beyond pointing the downloader at it
chaining: At $2.71 a month for an address with no byte meter and 100 Mbit/s, this is the cheapest residential-class egress in the set: it makes the total for a prohibited debrid service about $7 a month instead of $1,800.

limits.value: 1 GB bandwidth per address; shared by up to 3 users; no speed or concurrency upgrades on the basic plan

limits_note: 100 Mbit/s is 12.5 MB/s, or 1 TiB in 23.9 hours of saturated transfer; that is a throughput ceiling, not a volume ceiling, and it does not bind 1 TiB of monthly transfer.
binding_note: Nothing in the vocabulary fails at 1 TiB/month on this product: no byte meter, no concurrency limit below 100, and 100 Mbit/s clears the 3.24 Mbit/s 1 TiB of monthly transfer needs by a factor of 30.

identity_cost.detail: Checkout at app.proxy-cheap.com; card. No identity document was mentioned on the page read.

reliability_note: A static residential address is the class a debrid service is least equipped to refuse by inspection, and the class its terms most plainly name as a proxy.
confidence_note: Price, throughput and the unlimited-bandwidth bullet are on the vendor's pricing page read today. Whether the address is accepted by a given debrid service is inferred and untested.

notes: The single most important number among debrid providers: it is the counter-example to 'a residential proxy costs $2/GB and therefore debrid is pointless'. The metered market is $1.40-$6.00/GB; the static market is $0.30-$2.71 per IP per month with no meter. The two markets are different products and published records should never quote one as the price of the other.
